peak fields of 450 Oe effected little movement from their initial positions. It is concluded that these samples have been remagne- tized by lightning. KILBOURNE Tucson, Arizona 85719 Paleomagnetism of Some Rocks from the Mesaverde Group, Southwestern Wyoming and Northeastern Utah ABSTRACT The results of this investigation suggest that a viscous partial thermoremanent magnetization may be important for preserving paleomagnetic direc- tions in some sedimentary rocks. INTRODUCTION A paleomagnetic study of Upper Cretaceous (Campanian) sedimentary rocks of southwest- ern Wyoming and northeastern Utah demon- strates that rocks of weak intensity can be measured and useful information extracted from the data. Four different stratigraphic sections were sampled over a vertical interval whose location is shown on Figure 1, and the stratigraphy is summarized in Figure 2. Three magnetically oriented drill cores were collected stratigraphically at each 60-m vertical interval or as close to that interval as possible. Each core was cut into three specimens of length equal to its diameter in the laboratory. An astatic magnetometer was used to measure the directions and intensity of each specimen. ACKNOWLEDGMENTS The author gratefully acknowledges the assistance of Dr. R. L. Dubois, who directed this study, and Richard D. Champney.

The lower 550 feet of the formation were sampled in detail. Additional reconnaissance samples were taken at 10- to 30-foot intervals in the upper part of the formation, except that no samples were collected from the upper 120 feet of the formation. Since the Moenkopi Formation is approximately 1000 feet thick in this region, the detailed results presented below cover only about half of Moenkopi time. Samples collected during the initial search for reversals were cut to 1-inch cylinders in the field and measured in the field with a portable air-turbine spinner magnetometer (Helsley, 1967a). Subsequent samples taken in continuous stratigraphic sequence were cut to 1-inch cylinders upon return to the laboratory and were initially measured on the same air- turbine spinner magnetometer. Measurements made during the alternating current and ther- mal demagnetization experiments, including remeasurement of the initial magnetization, were made on a PAR SM-1 magnetometer. The alternating current demagnetization ex- periments were made on 420 cycle equipment similar to that described by Patton and Fitch (1962). All samples were tumbled about three axes during the AC demagnetization process in a region in which the residual D.C. field was less than 200 gammas. The applied AC field was varied smoothly from its maximum value to zero by precisely controlling the excitation current supplied to the 420 cycle motor-generator. COMPARISON WITH OTHER TRIASSIC POLES FOR NORTH AMERICA A summary of the Triassic pole positions for North America is given in Figure 11 and Table 8. The results of this study lie in the center of the main group of poles reported for other Triassic units (see Table 8 for references). The only pok position significantly removed from this main group is that of the New Oxford Formation (Graham, 1955) as reported by Irving (1964). ata from the Triassic Chugwater Formation in terms of lithologic types and in terms of normal and reversed intervals. He found that the distributions within normal and reversed groups were identical and that the only differences present were between lithologic types. His mean intensity for all samples was 6.5 X 10~ 6 emu/cc, and his range was from 0.6 to 70.4 X 10-6 emu/cc. Within the Moenkopi Formation, no rigor- ous attempt has been made to relate intensity of magnetization to lithologic type. The mean intensity of all samples is 4.56 X 10~6 emu/cc, and the range of intensities is from 0.31 to 53.2 X 10~ 6 emu/cc. Thermal demagnetization was accomplished in a conventional non-induclively wound elec- trical furnace, the samples being cooled in a region where the residual field was less than ±10 gammas. Temperature was monitored at each level of the furnace by means of platinum thermocouples that were referred to an ice bath and read on a digital voltmeter. Initial progressive AC demagnetization studies were made on about 10 percent of the samples with applied fields ranging from 44 to 1400 oersteds. This step-wise demagnetization showed that the magnetization was stable, that is, its intensity did not change rapidly with applied field, and that the coercive forces of the true NRM and any perturbing secondary components were approximately the same. Consequently, little decrease in scatter was accomplished as a result of the AC demagnet- ization experiments, as can be seen in the three sets of results given in Table 3. Since AC demagnetization had little effect on the observed directions of the NRM, progressive thermal demagnetization experi- ments were made on another set of samples selected primarily from the scattered portions of the reversed groups. These experiments produced large changes in the direction of magnetization, but only a small effect on the observed intensity until temperatures in excess of 600° C were reached. However, after thermal de- magnetization to 500° C, they become well clustered and have a direction approximately 180° from that of the normal intervals. All samples belong to either the normal or re- versed groups, and no samples transitional be- tween normal and reverse were observed. A tentative correlation of the resulting polarity reversal sequence with that from the Chugwater Formation of Wyoming is proposed. A magnetic anomaly pattern similar to this polarity reversal sequence is observed in magnetic profiles at sea, indicating that polarity reversal sequences may be a useful means of both regional correlation and calibration of the sea-floor spreading rates postu- lated for the ocean basins. INTRODUCTION For the Late Tertiary and Quaternary, polarity reversal sequences have been estab- lished in radiometrically dated kvas by Cox and others (1964). Similar polarity reversal sequences have been observed in deep-sea cores (for example, Opdyke and others, 1966; Wat- kins and Goodell, 1967). PREVIOUS WORK Observations made by Runcorn (1956), Kintzinger (1957), and Collinson and Runcorn (1960) have shown that rocks of Lower Triassic age in the western United States characteristi- cally have both normal and reversed polarities, although these authors did not attempt to define the polarity reversal sequence in these rock groups. The Lower Triassic Chugwater Formation of Wyoming has been more thor- oughly studied by Picard (1964); there he was able to find 11 magnetic zones (but only 7 polarity zones), some of which could appar- ently be correlated over large distances. GEOLOGIC SETTING The Moenkopi Formation crops out through- out the Colorado Plateau region in Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona, Utah, and Nevada. Its regional stratigraphy and history are discussed by McKee (1954). On the basis of regional correlation with other Permian and Triassic strata, Shoemaker and Newman (1959) conclude that the lowermost member of the Moenkopi may be either Permian or Triassic and that it is likely that the boundary lies within the lowest member. The uppermost units of the Moenkopi Formation are con- sidered by the same authors to be perhaps as young as Middle Triassic. section_candidates.excerpt: Triassic, 56" N, 100" E. Introduction Graham (1 955) noted the predominance of reversed directions in Permian red- beds of the western United States. A similar observation was made on the basis of a compilation of magnetic directions by Cox & Doell (1960). Following an examina- tion of Permian lavas in Australia in which only reversed magnetic directions were observed, Irving & Parry (1963) defined the Kiaman magnetic interval, and on the basis of published data from other continents, concluded that the interval extended from the beginning of Late Pennsylvanian time until approximately the close of the Palaeozoic Era. Although the information available from Europe and North America appears to support the presence of a prolonged field reversal, the division has previously been spanned only in the Australian section. In Australia the units studied represent only a small portion of the time interval involved (Irving 1966). The present study was undertaken with the express purpose of spanning the strati- graphic zone which corresponds to the Kiaman interval. We believe that the rock units represent as complete a depositional sequence as it will be possible to find within 265 L 266 a single depositional basin. laboratory procedures Samples were collected at stratigraphic intervals of 100 ft where possible, but the absence of suitable outcrops made it impossible to obtain this control at all locali- ties. A spinner magnetometer was used to measure the magnetic directions and intensities. In many cases it was necessary to spin the samples in field-free space to eliminate the effects of susceptibility anisotropy which could occasionally be detected. In addition it was necessary to spin most of the samples twice about each axis in order to get meaningful data. Richardson A modified Chevallier balance (Chevallier & Pierre 1932) has been used to determine the Curie points. The specimens, of approximate mass one hundred milli- grams, are heated rapidly in air, to inhibit oxidizing processes. Richardson (Received 1967 August 8) Summary The natural remanent magnetism of the Eocene Lisbon Volcanics has been determined using 39 samples from 12 lavas. The virtual geo- magnetic pole (207" E, 69" N, with dp = 7.7" and dm = 13.2") is significantly different from the mean Eocene geomagnetic pole for Europe. This result is consistent with previous independent suggestions of the creation of the Bay of Biscay by anticlockwise rotation of the Iberian peninsula, and implies therefore that the rotation was in part Post-Eocene. Alternatively, the Eocene geomagnetic field during the extrusion of the Lisbon Volcanics differed significantly from that recorded by other European Eocene rocks. Great between-island geomorphological contrasts characterize the islands. The very deeply dissected western slopes of Santa Antao are similar to parts of western Sao Nicolao and northern Sao Tiago. Younger, rounded topography is seen on any large scale only in eastern Santa Antao, and on Fogo, an island which is a single massive volcano rising to 2830 m above sea level. Conclusions Stable, consistent palaeomagnetic data have been obtained from 19 out of 31 sites in the Roraima Intrusive Suite (excluding four Group I11 sites, correlated with the Minor Dyke Suite of younger age, and the metadolerite at site 26). Fourteen of these sites fall into two groups of seven sites each, of distinctly and significantly different orientation. Representative samples from both groups are indistinguishable petrologically and in terms of bulk magnetic properties. This difference in magnetic polarity is considered to be primary, and to date from the time of emplacement and crystallization of sills of two different ages. It has survived a period of heating, possibly associated with the time of emplacement of the younger sills (which ever they may be), which caused substantial leakage of radiogenic argon and strontium from minerals in the rocks, to such an extent that they can no longer be distinguished by radiometric means. The suite is typically tholeitic, and the variety is such as is commonly encountered as a result of differentiation in thick dolerite hills. Some fine grained dolerites are definitely from the Minor Dyke Suite (samples at Site 24 were collected from the younger dykes which cut the main Tumatumari intrusion); others may well be chilled borders from the main Roraima Suite Intrusives. D. D. Hawkes (personal communication) has kindly examined thin sections representing most of the sites sampled in this study, and classified them according to the various stages in the differentiation sequence they are inferred to represent (see Hawkes (1966a), Table 1, p. 325). The stages he distinguishes range from early differentiates (norites and noritic dolerites), middle (pigeonite dolerite) to late (ferrodolerites). Hornblende granophyres represent heteromorphs of some pigeonite dolerites and ferrodolerites. The sites are classified petrologically in these terms, in Table 1. The progressive iron enrichment evidenced in this differentiation sequence is compatible with crystallization of basalt ma

ratios found (Hawkes op. cit.), and called for by this crystallization model. Sampling and measurement From two to eight orientated cores, averaging four inches in length, were obtained at each site by means of a portable gasoline-powered diamond drill (Doell & Cox 1967). The cores were oriented in situ with the aid of an astro-compass, (La Rochelle 1961). The three oriented hand samples from Cerro Bolivar were drilled in a press and reoriented in a sand-box. The remanence measurements were made on a spinner magnetometer (Phillips & Kuckes 1967); the alternating-field demagnetization apparatus is described by McElhinny (1963). The Curie Points and saturation magnetization measurements were made on a balance constructed by Collinson (1967). The maximum error, in orientation and measurement, is estimated to be less than 5". Results The palaeomagnetic results are summarized in Tables 1 and 2. Preliminary alter- nating field (a.f.) demagnetization of samples from several sites, in small increments up to 1000 Oe, showed 300 Oe to be the optimum field for routine demagnetization. Conclusions Stable, consistent palaeomagnetic data have been obtained from 19 out of 31 sites in the Roraima Intrusive Suite (excluding four Group I11 sites, correlated with the Minor Dyke Suite of younger age, and the metadolerite at site 26). Fourteen of these sites fall into two groups of seven sites each, of distinctly and significantly different orientation. Representative samples from both groups are indistinguishable petrologically and in terms of bulk magnetic properties. This difference in magnetic polarity is considered to be primary, and to date from the time of emplacement and crystallization of sills of two different ages. It has survived a period of heating, possibly associated with the time of emplacement of the younger sills (which ever they may be), which caused substantial leakage of radiogenic argon and strontium from minerals in the rocks, to such an extent that they can no longer be distinguished by radiometric means. The suite is typically tholeitic, and the variety is such as is commonly encountered as a result of differentiation in thick dolerite hills. Some fine grained dolerites are definitely from the Minor Dyke Suite (samples at Site 24 were collected from the younger dykes which cut the main Tumatumari intrusion); others may well be chilled borders from the main Roraima Suite Intrusives. D. D. Hawkes (personal communication) has kindly examined thin sections representing most of the sites sampled in this study, and classified them according to the various stages in the differentiation sequence they are inferred to represent (see Hawkes (1966a), Table 1, p. 325). The stages he distinguishes range from early differentiates (norites and noritic dolerites), middle (pigeonite dolerite) to late (ferrodolerites). Hornblende granophyres represent heteromorphs of some pigeonite dolerites and ferrodolerites. The sites are classified petrologically in these terms, in Table 1. The progressive iron enrichment evidenced in this differentiation sequence is compatible with crystallization of basalt ma

ratios found (Hawkes op. cit.), and called for by this crystallization model. Sampling and measurement From two to eight orientated cores, averaging four inches in length, were obtained at each site by means of a portable gasoline-powered diamond drill (Doell & Cox 1967). The cores were oriented in situ with the aid of an astro-compass, (La Rochelle 1961). The three oriented hand samples from Cerro Bolivar were drilled in a press and reoriented in a sand-box. The remanence measurements were made on a spinner magnetometer (Phillips & Kuckes 1967); the alternating-field demagnetization apparatus is described by McElhinny (1963). The Curie Points and saturation magnetization measurements were made on a balance constructed by Collinson (1967). The maximum error, in orientation and measurement, is estimated to be less than 5". Results The palaeomagnetic results are summarized in Tables 1 and 2. Preliminary alter- nating field (a.f.) demagnetization of samples from several sites, in small increments up to 1000 Oe, showed 300 Oe to be the optimum field for routine demagnetization. Conclusions Stable, consistent palaeomagnetic data have been obtained from 19 out of 31 sites in the Roraima Intrusive Suite (excluding four Group I11 sites, correlated with the Minor Dyke Suite of younger age, and the metadolerite at site 26). Fourteen of these sites fall into two groups of seven sites each, of distinctly and significantly different orientation. Representative samples from both groups are indistinguishable petrologically and in terms of bulk magnetic properties. This difference in magnetic polarity is considered to be primary, and to date from the time of emplacement and crystallization of sills of two different ages. It has survived a period of heating, possibly associated with the time of emplacement of the younger sills (which ever they may be), which caused substantial leakage of radiogenic argon and strontium from minerals in the rocks, to such an extent that they can no longer be distinguished by radiometric means. From west to east, on the line Belas-Olivais, we find a successive outcropping of Jurassic, Cretaceous, Eocene basalt flows, Oligocene Benfica formation and Miocene sediments. The author of the present paper has collected 22 samples from six sites, among which are four sites corresponding with Nos 6,7, 8 and 9 of Watkins & Richardson, of the same Lisbon volcanics. Their Table 5 (page 299) gives an elaborate statistical analysis; the mean direction of magnetization yielded a pole position of 207"E, 69"N (D: 347", I:+37", a95: ll", 39 samples, 12 flows). Particular emphasis was laid on laboratory methods, partly published in another paper as well (Watkins & Haggerty 1967). It should be noted, however, that Watkins & Richardson's suggestions regarding the undisturbed, flatlying position of the flows are not justified by field evidence. Though the basalt flows are badly exposed, the overlying Oligocene formations can be shown to have a moderate dip towards the east (Lisbon) or southeast (Odivelas, Loures). cks in North America are available from the south-west United States (Runcorn 1964, DuBois 1964), Montana (in Irving 1964), Missouri (Hays & Scharon 1966), and several parts of Canada (Fahrig et al. 1965). The samples fall into three distinct age groups (0-0.6 m.y., I m.y., and 2.0 m.y.), and the mean directions for these groups are in reasonable agreement with the values expected for a geo- centrio axial dipole field. An analysis of the group I data shows that the secular variation is consistent with the present day nondipole variation for the latitude of Runion. INTRODUCTION In recent years volcanic oceanic islands have been the subject of intensive geological and geophysical studies because of their increasing importance in many geophysical hypotheses. Studies have been made on islands in the Pa- cific Ocean, in particular the Hawaiian Islands, but little work has as yet been done on the islands in the Indian Ocean. The Masearene Islands, R6union, Mauritius, and Rodriguez, ap- peared to resemble the Hawaiian Islands in several respects; consequently, field work on these islands was undertaken by Ian MeDoug- all in July 1963 and a large number of orientated samples were collected for palcomagnetic work. The geology has been described by a number of authors, but the most recent account is given by Upton and Wadsworth [1965, 1966], whose nomenclature will be followed here. Fig- ure 1 is a geological sketch map of the island. Piton des Neiges, occupying the northwestern two-thirds of the island, has an over-all shield shape and is deeply dissected by gorges that have exposed the older formations. KNOWLES AND NElL D. OPDYKE Lamont Geological Observatory, Columbia University, Palisades, New York 10964 Specimens of red siltstone were collected at twenty-five sites in the Upper Mississippian Mauch Chunk formation of Pennsylvania. The sites were so distributed as to test whether the curve in the folded Appalachians was formed after the magnetization of the beds or whether the orginal geosyncline in Mississippian time was curved in plan. All specimens were partially demagnetized to isolate the stable component. When the beds are rotated back into a horizontal position, the stable components show a decrease in the scatter between the sites, indicating that the direction of magnetization was acquired before the folding of the Appa- lachians. The directions of demagnetization were found to be the same around the curve of the Appalachians, apparently ruling out their horizontal rotation after the acquisition of their stable magnetization. The pole position calculated from the Mauch Chunk is at 43øN, 127øE with a Ap -- 3.1, Am -- 6.3. This pole position is in general agreement with other late Paleo- zoic poles. JONES' Physics Department, University o/Alberta Edmonton, Alberta, Canada Sixteen samples of kimberlite have been collected from deep underground in the Premier Mine at Cullinan in the Transvaal. The stability of the natural remanent magnetization of the samples has been well tested by alternating-field demagnetization and confirmed by thermal demagnetization. The magnetization is shown to be associated with magnetite, some of which is of primary origin and some of secondary origin. The magnetite of secondary origin was formed contemporaneously with or shortly after the emplacement of the kimberlite as a result of extensive hydrothermal alteration of primary minerals. It has not been possible thus far to decide between a thermoremanent and a chemical remanent origin for the observed magnetization. ery great. INTRODUCTION In the Republic of South Africa there is a number of diamond-bearing kimberlite pipes. Economically, the most important occurrences are in the Kimberley region of the Cape Prov- ince and in an area to the northeast of Pretoria in the Transvaal. Mining operations have shown that the pipes of the Kimberley region intrude rocks of the Karroo system (Lower Carbonifer- ous to Lower Jurassic) of South Africa [du Toit, 1954]. They also contain inclusions of material derived from Karroo formations long since eroded away. There is thus no doubt that the pipes of the Kimberley area are post-Karroo in age and Williams [1932], referring to other writers, has suggested a mid-Cretaceous age of empIacement or even later. Of the pipes in the Pretoria area only one, that of the Premier Mine, has been exploited extensively. This pipe cuts no formations that have been positively identified as postdating the Bushveld igneous complex (1950 ñ 50 m.y. [Nicolaysen et al., 1958]), but it does contain a vast xenolith of Waterberg material. The Animikie sediments of the Mesabi Range (Fig. 3) strike at N70øE and dip at 6 ø to 12 ø to the southeast except around the Virginia syncline ./1 PALEOMAGNETIC STUDY ON IRON RANGES 1341 and Eveleth anticline. The sediments are cut by some minor gravity faults with displacements that rarely exceed 50 feet and associated minor drag folds. Two types of iron ore are nilned on the central Mesabi Range from within the Biwabik iron formation. The first, concentrating ore, contains coarse- grained magnetite in iron formation of the magnetite-banded oxide facies. The second, direct-shipping ore, contains soft martite and goethite with minor magnetite and specularite, and quartz as the major gangue mineral. The direct-shipping or soft ore is porous and friable, and it contains numerous slump structures. The soft ore deposits are found in areas of fracture such as anticlinal crests, and almost entirely within 500 feet of the surface. The ore bottoms on Pokegama quartzite or in unoxidized iron formation. The occurrence of the ore is unrelated to the Keweenawan dikes. SYMONS ABSTRACT One hundred and eleven samples of Animikie iron formation, partially altered iron formation, and direct-shipping iron ore %were collected from the Gunflint, Mesabi, and Cuyuna Ranges in the Lake Superior region of North America. Paleomagnctic measurements were made on the samples using an astatic magnetometer, and demagnetization by an alternating magnetic field was applied to test for remanence stability. The primary iron formations--the Gunflint, Biwabik, and Deerwood iron forma6ons from the Gunflint, Mesabi, and Cuyuna Ranges, respectively--appear to be contemporaneous with stable, primary chemical remanent magnetization (CRM) which, as indicated by the Gunflint iron formation, yields an Animkie paleomagnetic pole position of 94øVg, 28øN. The weathering hypothe- sis was proposed by Leith (24) in 1903, who suggested that meteoric solutions first oxidized the primary iron minerals, siderite and magnetite, in the iron formation to hematite and martite, respectively, and then they leached the silica from the iron formation to leave residual deposits of soft hematite and martite. Van Hise and Leith (42) in 1911 suggested further that the /alka- line groundwater solutions were derived from the surrounding granitic areas, and that the deposits were formed prior to the Cambrian period and for the most part during the Upper Animikie. Wolff (46) in 1915 and Zapffe (47) in 1928 have supported the hypothesis of Van Hise and Leith in discussing the Mesabi and Cuyuna Ranges, respectively. Royce(33) in 1942 favored the weathering hypothesis except that he believed that the ores were formed for the most part after the Cretaceous period or in the present erosion cycle.
